content: The information was made available on the WHO website for public notice and comment. No additional details regarding potential conflicts of interest or biases related to the individuals being considered for membership in the guideline development group were identified through the public notice process. The guideline focuses on protecting, promoting, and supporting breastfeeding in facilities that provide maternity and newborn services. The initial set of questions to be addressed in the guidelines served as the foundation for formulating the recommendations. These questions were drafted by technical staff from the Evidence and Programme Guidance Unit of the Department of Nutrition for Health and Development, based on the policy and programmatic needs of Member States and their partners. The questions were subsequently reviewed and discussed by the steering group. A meeting of the guideline development group was held from April 11–13, 2016, in Geneva, Switzerland, to finalize the scope of the questions and prioritize the outcomes and populations of interest for the recommendations on breastfeeding in maternity and newborn care facilities. The group evaluated the relevance of the questions and made modifications as necessary. They also scored the importance of each outcome on a scale from 1 to 9, where scores of 7–9 indicated critical importance, 4–6 indicated moderate importance, and 1–3 indicated low importance. The final key questions and critical outcomes for decision-making were documented in PICO format and included in Annex 1. To identify evidence, a search for previous systematic reviews addressing the key questions was conducted in databases such as the Campbell Collaboration, Cochrane Library, EMBASE, Epistemonikos, Health Systems Evidence, MEDLINE, and the WHO Global Index Medicus, up to December 2015. A total of 52 systematic reviews were identified and assessed for relevance, quality, and timeliness. Of these, nine were from the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group, seven from the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group, and two from independent publications. Updates to these systematic reviews were commissioned to the original authors. Additionally, four PICO questions were assigned to St. Luke’s International University in Tokyo, Japan, as part of the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group. In total, 22 systematic reviews were updated or developed to inform the recommendations, with details provided in Annex 2. The WHO Secretariat also conducted a qualitative evidence synthesis of published literature to summarize research on maternal values, preferences, and factors influencing acceptability among health workers and stakeholders. Further searches were performed to gather information on resource use, feasibility, equity, and human rights issues for each intervention. Systematic reviews based on the PICO questions were used to summarize and appraise the evidence, following the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions. Each study included in the reviews was assessed for risk of bias, which contributed to the overall quality assessment of the evidence. During discussions, the steering group and guideline development group carefully reviewed the quality, scope, and inclusion criteria of the systematic reviews. The relative weight of randomized and non-randomized studies was considered in the quality assessment. When possible, findings were synthesized into pooled estimates of effect. The results of the systematic reviews, along with confidence assessments in the effect estimates for critical outcomes, were presented to the guideline development group. Evidence profiles were prepared using the GRADE approach to assess the overall quality of evidence, which was rated as high, moderate, low, or very low based on criteria such as risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision, indirectness, and publication bias. Summaries of findings are available in Annex 3. The findings of qualitative reviews on maternal values, preferences, and acceptability of breastfeeding interventions among health workers were appraised using the GRADE-CERQual approach. Overall confidence in the evidence from qualitative research was based on methodological limitations, data adequacy, coherence, and relevance. Summaries of qualitative findings on maternal values and preferences are in Annex 4, while those on acceptability among health workers and stakeholders are in Annex 5. The draft recommendations were discussed by the steering group and the guideline development group during a meeting held from November 7–11, 2016, in Florence, Italy. Three types of recommendations were agreed upon: recommended, recommended only in specific contexts, and not recommended. A recommended intervention is one where the desirable consequences clearly outweigh the undesirable ones, and most individuals would likely choose the recommended course of action. For health-care workers, this implies that most individuals should receive the intervention. For policymakers, it suggests that the recommendation can be adopted as a policy, quality standard, or performance indicator in most situations. Recommendations recommended only in specific contexts indicate that the balance of benefits and harms may vary depending on the situation. These recommendations specify the contexts in which they apply. Systematic reviews and GRADE evidence profiles for critical outcomes were used to draft recommendations. An evidence-to-decision framework guided discussions and decision-making, considering domains such as quality of evidence, balance of benefits and harms, values and preferences, acceptability, resource implications, feasibility, and equity. The quality of evidence, as presented in the GRADE profiles, was a key factor in drafting recommendations. Higher-quality evidence across critical outcomes increased the likelihood of a clear positive recommendation. The balance of benefits and harms was evaluated, including the magnitude and relative importance of effects. Clear benefits or harms led to stronger recommendations, while uncertainty often resulted in context-specific recommendations. The steering group reviewed qualitative information on how end-users (mothers) perceived breastfeeding interventions and presented this during the guideline development group meeting. When there was uncertainty or variability in values and preferences, context-specific recommendations were considered. Acceptability among health-care workers and service providers was also reviewed, with higher acceptability increasing the likelihood of a recommendation. Strategies to address low acceptability during implementation were discussed when necessary. Resource implications were evaluated to determine the cost-effectiveness and resource intensity of interventions. Clear advantages or disadvantages in resource use influenced recommendations, while uncertainty justified context-specific recommendations. Feasibility was assessed by presenting examples of breastfeeding interventions implemented in various settings, highlighting barriers and facilitators. Greater feasibility increased the likelihood of a recommendation. Equity and human rights considerations were also critical. Interventions likely to reduce health inequities among vulnerable groups were more likely to be recommended. Each recommendation was supported by a rationale, implementation considerations, and research priorities. Consensus decision-making procedures were established at the beginning of the meetings. At least two-thirds of the guideline development group needed to be present for discussions. Decisions were made through secret ballot voting, with no abstentions allowed. If unanimous consensus was not reached, further deliberations and a second round of voting were conducted. A two-thirds majority was required for approval if consensus was not achieved. Voting results will be retained by WHO for up to five years. The guideline document was prepared by the responsible technical officer, with input from the steering group. It underwent technical editing and proofreading by a contracted party. The final draft was peer-reviewed by content experts to ensure accuracy, address omissions or inconsistencies, and clarify language. Independent peer reviewers were selected by the steering group, with 16 agreeing to participate. Comments were reviewed, and the document was revised to maintain clarity and consistency with the original meaning. The guideline will be disseminated through the WHO website, including the WHO Nutrition website and the e-Library of Evidence for Nutrition Actions (eLENA). It will also be shared through a network of international partners, including WHO offices, ministries of health, collaborating centers, universities, UN agencies, and NGOs. An implementation guide encompassing the recommendations, the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes, and the Baby-friendly Hospital Initiative will be published separately. The WHO steering group will monitor research developments in breastfeeding support and update the guideline as needed, particularly for areas with low-quality evidence. Updates will follow the formal procedures outlined in the WHO handbook for guideline development. As the guideline approaches its 10-year review period, a search for new evidence will be conducted by the Department of Nutrition for Health and Development at WHO headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland, in collaboration with internal partners.
